v.q: A downstream service becomes slow but does not fail. Why is this worse than it being down?
o: Callers wait and hold threads, so the slowness cascades up the chain
Slow services always return wrong data
A slow service cannot be retried or monitored
Slowness only affects the first caller
v.w: A failing service fails fast. A slow one ties up threads and connections in every caller, which become slow in turn.

v.q: Which situation is a cascading failure?
o: A slow call ties up caller threads
A service restarts once
A log line is missing
One request returns 404
v.w: Waiting callers use up threads, so the slowness spreads up the chain of services.

v.q: Three layers each retry a failing call three times. How many calls can one request create?
o: Up to 27 calls, a retry storm
Exactly 3 calls
9 calls, because retries are not multiplied
Only 1 call, because retries are merged
v.w: Retries multiply across layers. Retry at one layer, cap attempts, add backoff and jitter and a retry budget.

v.q: Two layers each retry a failing call twice. How many calls can one request become at the bottom?
o: Up to 9
Exactly 2
Exactly 4
Only 1
v.w: Each of three attempts on the first layer triggers three on the next, so retries multiply instead of adding.

v.q: Which requests are safe to retry automatically?
o: Idempotent calls that failed with a transient error such as a timeout or 503
Every call that returned a 400 or 404 error
Payment POST requests without an idempotency key
Only calls that succeeded on the first attempt
v.w: Retrying a non-idempotent call can charge twice, and client errors will simply fail again.

v.q: Which request is NOT safe to retry automatically?
o: A payment POST with no idempotency key
A GET that timed out
A PUT that returned 503
A DELETE that timed out
v.w: The first attempt may have worked, so a retry can charge twice unless the server can recognise it.

v.q: What happens in the open state of a circuit breaker?
o: Calls fail immediately or use a fallback for a wait time
All calls pass through while failures are counted
A few trial calls are sent to test recovery
The dependency is restarted by the breaker
v.w: Open protects the caller and gives the sick service quiet to recover. After the wait the breaker becomes half-open and probes.

v.q: Which circuit breaker state counts failures while letting calls through?
o: Closed
Open
Half-open
Disabled
v.w: Closed is the normal state. It opens when the failure rate passes a threshold.

v.q: What problem does a bulkhead solve?
o: One slow dependency using all threads and starving other calls
Duplicate messages delivered by a broker
Expired tokens at the gateway
Stale entries in a service registry
v.w: Each dependency gets its own limited pool or concurrency cap, so excess calls are rejected quickly and other work continues.

v.q: Which pool design best isolates a slow dependency?
o: A separate thread pool per dependency
One shared pool for every call
A bigger shared pool
No timeout on calls
v.w: A bulkhead gives each dependency its own limit, so one cannot take all the threads.

v.q: What is the main purpose of jitter in a retry policy?
o: Spread retries out so clients do not all retry at the same moment
Make each retry wait exactly the same time
Increase the number of retry attempts
Hide the failure from the circuit breaker
v.w: Random variation added to the backoff prevents waves of simultaneous retries, a thundering herd, against a recovering service.

v.q: Which retry delay pattern avoids clients retrying together?
o: Backoff with jitter
A fixed delay
No delay
A delay equal to the timeout
v.w: Random spread stops thousands of clients from retrying at the same instant.

v.q: A service is overloaded by a traffic spike. What is the better response?
o: Reject excess low-priority requests early with 429 or 503
Queue every request with no limit so none are lost
Increase client timeouts so requests can wait longer
Retry every rejected request immediately
v.w: Unbounded queues hide overload until every request is too old to matter. Shedding keeps accepted requests fast.

v.q: Which response is NOT good load shedding?
o: Accept and queue everything without limit
Reject low-priority work early
Return 429 with Retry-After
Protect critical requests first
v.w: An unbounded queue turns overload into long delays and memory exhaustion.

v.q: Why should a liveness probe not check the database?
o: A database outage would restart every healthy instance and make things worse
Databases cannot answer health queries
Liveness probes run only once at startup
It would hide the failure from the readiness probe
v.w: Liveness is about whether this process is stuck. Dependencies belong in readiness, which only removes the pod from traffic.

v.q: Which check belongs in a readiness probe, not in a liveness probe?
o: Can the service reach the database?
Is the process responding?
Is the JVM alive?
Is the event loop running?
v.w: An unready pod is only removed from traffic. A failing liveness probe restarts it, which would not fix a database outage.
